claim: The vertebrate 'neural plate border' is a transient territory located at the edge of the neural plate containing precursors for all ectodermal derivatives: the neural plate, neural crest, placodes and epidermis.
source: The vertebrate 'neural plate border' is a transient territory located at the edge of the neural plate containing precursors for all ectodermal derivatives: the neural plate, neural crest, placodes and epidermis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the neural plate border as containing multiple precursor types.

claim: Single cell RNA sequencing was performed on chick ectoderm from primitive streak to neurulation stage to explore cell state diversity and heterogeneity.
source: Here, we carry out single cell RNA sequencing of chick ectoderm from primitive streak to neurulation stage, to explore cell state diversity and heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Genes previously classified as neural plate border 'specifiers' typically exhibit dynamic expression patterns and are enriched in either neural, neural crest or placodal fates.
source: Furthermore, we find that genes previously classified as neural plate border 'specifiers' typically exhibit dynamic expression patterns and are enriched in either neural, neural crest or placodal fates, revealing that the neural plate border should be seen as a heterogeneous ectodermal territory and not a discrete transitional transcriptional state.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene module analysis and expression dynamics modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The neural plate border should be seen as a heterogeneous ectodermal territory and not a discrete transitional transcriptional state.
source: Furthermore, we find that genes previously classified as neural plate border 'specifiers' typically exhibit dynamic expression patterns and are enriched in either neural, neural crest or placodal fates, revealing that the neural plate border should be seen as a heterogeneous ectodermal territory and not a discrete transitional transcriptional state.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of gene expression patterns and cell state classifications.

claim: Individual NPB cells co-express competing transcriptional programmes suggesting that their ultimate identity is not yet fixed.
source: Analysis of neural, neural crest and placodal markers reveals that individual NPB cells co-express competing transcriptional programmes suggesting that their ultimate identify is not yet fixed.
evidence: This is supported by the co-expression analysis of gene modules shown in Figure 6.

claim: A population of 'border located undecided progenitors' (BLUPs) gradually diminishes as cell fate decisions take place.
source: This population of 'border located undecided progenitors' (BLUPs) gradually diminishes as cell fate decisions take place.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-expression analysis across developmental stages showing decreasing numbers of cells co-expressing multiple fate modules.

claim: The probability of a progenitor's daughters to contribute to a given ectodermal derivative is related to the balance of competing transcriptional programmes.
source: Our data suggest that the probability of a progenitor's daughters to contribute to a given ectodermal derivative is related to the balance of competing transcriptional programmes, which in turn are regulated by the spatiotemporal position of a progenitor.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observed graded expression patterns and co-expression of gene modules.

claim: The balance of competing transcriptional programmes is regulated by the spatiotemporal position of a progenitor.
source: Our data suggest that the probability of a progenitor's daughters to contribute to a given ectodermal derivative is related to the balance of competing transcriptional programmes, which in turn are regulated by the spatiotemporal position of a progenitor.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial modeling of gene expression across the mediolateral axis and validation by HCR.

claim: Neural crest cells form along the entire body axis to generate various cell types including neurons and glial as well as parts of the craniofacial skeleton, cartilage, and teeth.
source: Placode derivatives are confined to the head contributing to sense organs and cranial ganglia, while neural crest cells form along the entire body axis to generate various cell types including neurons and glial as well as parts of the craniofacial skeleton, cartilage, and teeth (for review: Baker and Bronner-Fraser, 1997a; Baker and Bronner-Fraser, 2001; Grocott et al., 2012; Patthey et al., 2014; Pla and Monsoro-Burq, 2018; Prasad et al., 2019; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple review citations.

claim: Placode derivatives are confined to the head contributing to sense organs and cranial ganglia.
source: Placode derivatives are confined to the head contributing to sense organs and cranial ganglia, while neural crest cells form along the entire body axis to generate various cell types including neurons and glial as well as parts of the craniofacial skeleton, cartilage, and teeth (for review: Baker and Bronner-Fraser, 1997a; Baker and Bronner-Fraser, 2001; Grocott et al., 2012; Patthey et al., 2014; Pla and Monsoro-Burq, 2018; Prasad et al., 2019; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple review citations.

claim: The neural plate border contains a mixture of neural, neural crest, placodal, and epidermal precursors.
source: Lineage tracing has shown that the NPB contains a mixture of neural, neural crest, placodal, and epidermal precursors (Bhattacharyya et al., 2004; Bronner-Fraser and Fraser, 1988; Dutta et al., 2005; Kozlowski et al., 1997; Pieper et al., 2011; Streit, 2002; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lineage tracing studies cited.

claim: FGF signalling is required for the specification of neural, neural crest and placode precursors and for positioning the NPB.
source: FGF signalling is required for the specification of neural, neural crest and placode precursors and for positioning the NPB (Ahrens and Schlosser, 2005; Litsiou et al., 2005; Londin et al., 2005; Monsoro-Burq et al., 2003; Streit et al., 2000; Streit and Stern, 1999; Stuhlmiller and García-Castro, 2012; Wilson et al., 2000; Yardley and García-Castro, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on FGF signaling.

claim: BMP signalling must be inhibited for neural development.
source: While BMP signalling must be inhibited for neural development (Hemmati-Brivanlou et al., 1994; Linker and Stern, 2004; Londin et al., 2005; Sasai et al., 1995), it is necessary for placode precursor formation at gastrulation, but must be switched off thereafter (Ahrens and Schlosser, 2005; Kwon et al., 2010; Litsiou et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on BMP signaling.

claim: BMP signalling is necessary for placode precursor formation at gastrulation, but must be switched off thereafter.
source: While BMP signalling must be inhibited for neural development (Hemmati-Brivanlou et al., 1994; Linker and Stern, 2004; Londin et al., 2005; Sasai et al., 1995), it is necessary for placode precursor formation at gastrulation, but must be switched off thereafter (Ahrens and Schlosser, 2005; Kwon et al., 2010; Litsiou et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on BMP signaling in placode development.

claim: Neural crest cells need BMP activity early and continue to require it as they are firmly established.
source: Likewise, neural crest cells need BMP activity early, but unlike placodes, continue to do so as they are firmly established (Barth et al., 1999; Kwon et al., 2010; Liem et al., 1995; Marchant et al., 1998; Steventon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on BMP signaling in neural crest development.

claim: Wnt activity is required for neural crest cell induction.
source: Finally, Wnt activity is required for neural crest cell induction (García-Castro et al., 2002; Steventon et al., 2009) but must be inhibited for neural and placode precursors to form (Heeg-Truesdell and LaBonne, 2006; Litsiou et al., 2005; Patthey et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Wnt signaling in neural crest induction.

claim: Wnt activity must be inhibited for neural and placode precursors to form.
source: Finally, Wnt activity is required for neural crest cell induction (García-Castro et al., 2002; Steventon et al., 2009) but must be inhibited for neural and placode precursors to form (Heeg-Truesdell and LaBonne, 2006; Litsiou et al., 2005; Patthey et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Wnt signaling in neural and placode development.

claim: Msx1 and Pax3 have been implicated as NPB specifiers.
source: For example, Msx1 and Pax3 have been implicated as NPB specifiers (Milet et al., 2013; Monsoro-Burq, 2015; Plouhinec et al., 2014), whereas Pax7 (Basch et al., 2006) and Six1 (Brugmann et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2009; Christophorou et al., 2009; Ozaki et al., 2004) control neural crest and placode precursor formation, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on NPB specifier genes.

claim: Pax7 controls neural crest precursor formation.
source: For example, Msx1 and Pax3 have been implicated as NPB specifiers (Milet et al., 2013; Monsoro-Burq, 2015; Plouhinec et al., 2014), whereas Pax7 (Basch et al., 2006) and Six1 (Brugmann et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2009; Christophorou et al., 2009; Ozaki et al., 2004) control neural crest and placode precursor formation, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on Pax7 function.

claim: Six1 controls placode precursor formation.
source: For example, Msx1 and Pax3 have been implicated as NPB specifiers (Milet et al., 2013; Monsoro-Burq, 2015; Plouhinec et al., 2014), whereas Pax7 (Basch et al., 2006) and Six1 (Brugmann et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2009; Christophorou et al., 2009; Ozaki et al., 2004) control neural crest and placode precursor formation, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on Six1 function.

claim: The 'binary competence model' proposes that the NPB territory is rapidly subdivided into neural/neural crest competent and placode/epidermal competent ectoderm.
source: The 'binary competence model' proposes that while a territory containing neural crest and placodal precursors exists at the time of gastrulation, this territory is rapidly subdivided into neural/neural crest competent and placode/epidermal competent ectoderm through changes in the regulatory relationships of the transcription factors expressed (sequence of cell fate decisions: [epidermal-placodal]-[NC-neural]) (Ahrens and Schlosser, 2005; Pieper et al., 2012; Schlosser, 2014; Maharana and Schlosser, 2018).
evidence: This is a description of a model proposed in cited literature.

claim: The 'NPB model' suggests that cells at the border of the neural plate have mixed identity and retain the ability to generate all ectodermal derivatives until after neurulation begins.
source: In contrast, the 'NPB model' suggests that cells at the border of the neural plate have mixed identity and retain the ability to generate all ectodermal derivatives until after neurulation begins (Baker and Bronner-Fraser, 1997b; Roellig et al., 2017; Streit and Stern, 1999).
evidence: This is a description of a model proposed in cited literature.

claim: Cells at the NPB retain pluripotency markers which is key for their multipotency.
source: Other studies in Xenopus have taken this idea a step further, revealing that unlike other ectodermal cells, cells at the NPB retain pluripotency markers which is key for their multipotency (Buitrago-Delgado et al., 2015; Prasad et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies in Xenopus.

claim: Studies in chick have begun to characterise cell heterogeneity at the NPB at a single-cell level revealing that factors previously thought to be fate-specific are co-expressed in individual cells even at late neural tube stages.
source: Studies in chick have begun to characterise cell heterogeneity at the NPB at a single-cell level revealing that factors previously thought to be fate-specific are co-expressed in individual cells even at late neural tube stages (Roellig et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies in chick.

claim: Classical lineage tracing reveals that individual ectodermal cells can give rise to both neural and neural crest even at fairly late stages.
source: Furthermore, classical lineage tracing reveals that individual ectodermal cells can give rise to both neural and neural crest even at fairly late stages (Bronner-Fraser and Fraser, 1988), while more a more recent study using a neural-specific Sox2 enhancer shows that Sox2+ cells can contribute not only to neural tissue but also to neural crest and epidermis (Roellig et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited lineage tracing studies.

claim: Sox2+ cells can contribute not only to neural tissue but also to neural crest and epidermis.
source: Furthermore, classical lineage tracing reveals that individual ectodermal cells can give rise to both neural and neural crest even at fairly late stages (Bronner-Fraser and Fraser, 1988), while more a more recent study using a neural-specific Sox2 enhancer shows that Sox2+ cells can contribute not only to neural tissue but also to neural crest and epidermis (Roellig et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study using Sox2 enhancer lineage tracing.

claim: A total of 17,992 high-quality cells were captured in the scRNAseq dataset.
source: After integration across batches, stringent quality control and removal of contaminating cell populations (see Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-I ), we captured a total of 17,992 high-quality cells with approximately 2500–4000 cells per stage and an average of 3924 genes per cell.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data collected.

claim: An average of 3924 genes per cell were detected in the scRNAseq dataset.
source: After integration across batches, stringent quality control and removal of contaminating cell populations (see Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-I ), we captured a total of 17,992 high-quality cells with approximately 2500–4000 cells per stage and an average of 3924 genes per cell.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data quality metric.

claim: Cells at later stages displayed higher cell diversity compared with earlier stages where most cells were transcriptionally similar.
source: Dimensionality reduction and UMAP embedding reveals that cells at later stages displayed higher cell diversity compared with earlier stages where most cells were transcriptionally similar (Figure 2B–E and Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP visualizations showing increasing separation of cell clusters at later stages.

claim: A binary knowledge matrix based on expression data obtained from the literature was used to categorise cells.
source: To overcome these challenges, we categorised cells using a binary knowledge matrix based on expression data obtained from the literature (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used for cell classification.

claim: 76 genes with known regionalised expression patterns were examined to define 24 cell states spanning primitive streak to neural tube stages.
source: We examined available in situ hybridisation data of 76 genes with known regionalised expression patterns and binarized their expression within each defined cell state. This allowed us to define a total of 24 cell states spanning primitive streak to neural tube stages.
evidence: This describes the construction of the binary knowledge matrix.

claim: Early NPB and early neural cell populations can already be identified at primitive streak stages.
source: This classification approach successfully identified 22 distinct cell states within the ectoderm across all developmental stages. Early NPB and early neural cell populations can already be identified at primitive streak stages, while placode progenitor and neural crest states emerge at head process and ss4, respectively (Figure 2B and Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the cell state classifications shown in the figures.

claim: Placode progenitor states emerge at head process stage.
source: This classification approach successfully identified 22 distinct cell states within the ectoderm across all developmental stages. Early NPB and early neural cell populations can already be identified at primitive streak stages, while placode progenitor and neural crest states emerge at head process and ss4, respectively (Figure 2B and Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the cell state classifications shown in the figures.

claim: Neural crest states emerge at ss4.
source: This classification approach successfully identified 22 distinct cell states within the ectoderm across all developmental stages. Early NPB and early neural cell populations can already be identified at primitive streak stages, while placode progenitor and neural crest states emerge at head process and ss4, respectively (Figure 2B and Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the cell state classifications shown in the figures.

claim: At HH4, five cell states were identified: node, early neural (eN), early neural plate border (eNPB), non-neural ectoderm (NNE) and extraembryonic ectoderm (EE).
source: Cell states can be broadly characterised based on combinatorial gene expression (Figure 2) and we identify five cell states: node, early neural (eN), early neural plate border (eNPB), non-neural ectoderm (NNE) and extraembryonic ectoderm (EE) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An early NPB population co-expresses both neural and non-neural genes.
source: Notably, we identify an early NPB population which co-expresses both neural and non-neural genes.
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression analysis at HH4.

claim: Early NPB cells are apparent prior to the differential upregulation of genes previously characterised as NPB specifiers.
source: Thus, early NPB cells are already apparent prior to the differential upregulation of genes previously characterised as NPB specifiers (Msx1, Pax7, Tfap2a, Dlx5/6, Pax3) (Hong et al., 2007; Maharana and Schlosser, 2018; Monsoro-Burq et al., 2005; Pla and Monsoro-Burq, 2018) (for review: Sauka-Spengler and Bronner-Fraser, 2008; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Thiery et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the observation of eNPB cells at HH4 before upregulation of NPB specifiers.

claim: At HH5, the upregulation of PPR genes (Six1, Eya2) is observed for the first time.
source: At HH6, GM12 is downregulated in the NPB and remains confined to the PPR clusters until ss8. Unlike GM12, GM14 is initially restricted to the PPR and only activated in the pNPB at HH7. At ss4 and ss8 its expression is confined to the PPR, with a higher expression in anterior cells.
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression analysis at HH5.

claim: So-called NPB specifiers (Msx1, Pax3, Pax7) are first observed at HH5.
source: However, at HH5 we observe the upregulation of PPR genes (Six1, Eya2; Figure 2C and E: aPPR, anterior PPR) and for the first time so-called NPB specifiers (Msx1, Pax3, Pax7; Figure 2C and E: pNPB, posterior NPB).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in the figures.

claim: The NPB initially has a posterior character, while placode precursors have anterior identity based on their expression of Gbx2 and Six3, respectively.
source: Notably, the NPB initially has a posterior character, while placode precursors have anterior identity based on their expression of Gbx2 and Six3, respectively (Figure 2E; see also below).
evidence: This is supported by the expression patterns of Gbx2 and Six3 shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cells with distinct anteroposterior (A-P) character are first observed at HH5 through the restricted expression of various homeobox transcription factors.
source: Cells with distinct anteroposterior (A-P) character are first observed at HH5 through the restricted expression of various homeobox transcription factors.
evidence: This is supported by the expression analysis of homeobox genes at HH5.

claim: At HH7, two major superclusters are identified, one containing neural tube and neural crest and the other placodal and future epidermal clusters.
source: Following clustering, we identified two major superclusters at HH7, one containing neural tube and neural crest and the other placodal and future epidermal clusters (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neural crest cells first emerge as a distinct cell population at HH7.
source: Thus, neural crest cells first emerge as a distinct cell population at HH7.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of a neural crest cluster expressing definitive markers at HH7.

claim: Msx1 and Pax7 are not strongly expressed within placodal cell clusters but instead are enriched in neural crest progenitors.
source: Furthermore, we find that Msx1 and Pax7 are not strongly expressed within placodal cell clusters but instead are enriched in neural crest progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by the expression analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At ss4 and ss8, a NPB cell cluster can no longer be identified.
source: At ss4 and ss8, a NPB cell cluster can no longer be identified using the above criteria.
evidence: This is based on the cell state classification at these stages.

claim: At ss4 and ss8, an increasing diversity of cells classified as placodal, neural crest or neural is observed.
source: Instead, we observe an increasing diversity of cells classified as placodal, neural crest or neural (Figure 3B, C and E).
evidence: This is shown in the UMAP plots and cell state classifications.

claim: Within the neural cell population, forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain (FB, MB, HB) clusters are clearly distinguishable at ss4.
source: Within the neural cell population, forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain (FB, MB, HB) clusters are clearly distinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by the cell state classifications and marker expression at ss4.

claim: Small cell populations connect PPR, neural crest, forebrain and midbrain clusters at ss4 and ss8, in a four-way pattern reflecting their A-P and M-L segregation in vivo.
source: Despite the apparent segregation of neural, neural crest and placodal cell states at ss4 and ss8, small cell populations connect PPR, neural crest, forebrain and midbrain clusters, in a four-way pattern reflecting their A-P and M-L segregation in vivo (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the UMAP plots at ss4 and ss8.

claim: RNA velocity analysis predicts that connecting cell populations move away from cluster boundaries, towards definitive cell states.
source: To predict the directionality of transcriptional change within these populations, and hence their potential developmental trajectory, we performed RNA velocity analysis (Bergen et al., 2020; La Manno et al., 2018). This analysis predicts that they move away from cluster boundaries, towards definitive cell states (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is based on RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Fate restricted markers are upregulated from HH5 onwards.
source: Together our data show that whereas cell states at HH4-HH6 exhibit broad overlapping gene expression, fate restricted markers are upregulated from HH5 onwards.
evidence: This is a summary of the gene expression dynamics observed across stages.

claim: At HH7 and ss4, placodal, neural crest and neural states begin to segregate.
source: At HH7 and ss4, placodal, neural crest and neural states begin to segregate.
evidence: This is supported by the emergence of distinct cell clusters at these stages.

claim: Even as the neural tube closes, cells continue to straddle cluster boundaries and may be transcriptionally undecided.
source: However, even as the neural tube closes, cells continue to straddle cluster boundaries; these cells may be transcriptionally undecided and therefore still actively undergoing fate decision processes.
evidence: This is based on the observation of cells at cluster boundaries in the UMAP plots.

claim: 40 gene modules were calculated using the Antler R package showing highly correlated gene expression across all stages (HH4-ss8).
source: Gene modules are groups of genes that display similar expression profiles across a dataset. We calculated gene modules using the Antler R package (Delile et al., 2019), which iteratively clusters genes hierarchically based on their gene-gene Spearman correlation. This approach reveals 40 modules each showing highly correlated gene expression across all stages (HH4-ss8).
evidence: This describes the gene module calculation approach and results.

claim: Nine gene modules were identified that show differential expression between at least one of the three fates (neural, neural crest, placodal) at ss8.
source: Finally, since our data show that the segregation of neural, neural crest and placodal cell states is almost complete at ss8 (Figure 3C), we kept those gene modules that show differential expression between at least one of the three fates at ss8 (see Materials and methods). This resulted in nine modules that were considered further ( Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the filtering process for gene modules.

claim: Four gene modules (GM21-24) are specifically expressed in the PPR at ss8.
source: Of these, four gene modules (GM21-24) are specifically expressed in the PPR at ss8, one (GM13) in neural crest cells, and the remaining four (GM7, 9, 11, 20) are upregulated primarily in neural clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the gene module heatmap in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: One gene module (GM13) is specifically expressed in neural crest cells at ss8.
source: Of these, four gene modules (GM21-24) are specifically expressed in the PPR at ss8, one (GM13) in neural crest cells, and the remaining four (GM7, 9, 11, 20) are upregulated primarily in neural clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the gene module heatmap in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Four gene modules (GM7, 9, 11, 20) are upregulated primarily in neural clusters at ss8.
source: Of these, four gene modules (GM21-24) are specifically expressed in the PPR at ss8, one (GM13) in neural crest cells, and the remaining four (GM7, 9, 11, 20) are upregulated primarily in neural clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the gene module heatmap in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GM9 contains neural markers like Lmo1 and Sox21.
source: GM9 becomes upregulated in all neural clusters and includes neural markers like Lmo1 and Sox21 (Figure 4E 'Neural GM9', Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the gene module analysis.

claim: GM13 contains well known neural crest markers Pax7, Snai2, Sox10, and Tfap2b.
source: In contrast, modelling reveals that GM13 is upregulated in cells with neural crest identity. Indeed, it contains well known neural crest markers Pax7, Snai2, Sox10, and Tfap2b (Figure 4E 'NC GM13', Figure 4—source data 1) and is initially broadly activated in NPB and neural crest clusters at HH7.
evidence: This is stated and shown in the gene module analysis.

claim: GM23 contains bona fide placodal genes like Six1 and Eya2.
source: Finally, modelling the expression dynamics of GM23 shows that it is activated early and becomes upregulated in cells with placodal character across latent time. This prediction is supported by the fact that GM23 is highly expressed in PPR clusters at ss8 and contains bona fide placodal genes like Six1 and Eya2 (Figure 4E 'Placodal GM23', Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the gene module analysis.

claim: The placodal gene module (GM23) is activated first, followed by the neural (GM9) and neural crest (GM13) gene modules.
source: Comparing the onset of activation of these three gene modules across latent time reveals a clear temporal order with the placodal module being activated first, followed by the neural and neural crest gene modules.
evidence: This is based on the gene module dynamics modeling across latent time.

claim: GM24 and GM21 are initially expressed in all three cell populations (neural, neural crest, placodal) before being rapidly downregulated within neural crest and neural cells.
source: In contrast to these modules, modelling of GM24 and GM21 shows that they are initially expressed in all three cell populations before being rapidly downregulated within neural crest and neural cells (Figure 4E 'Epiblast GM21' and 'Epiblast GM24').
evidence: This is shown in the gene module dynamics plots in Figure 4E.

claim: Genes in GM24 are broadly expressed across the epiblast at HH4, and then become gradually restricted to PPR, non-neural and NPB clusters at HH6/7, and to PPR cells at ss4/8.
source: Indeed, genes in GM24 are broadly expressed across the epiblast at HH4, and then become gradually restricted to PPR, non-neural and NPB clusters at HH6/7, and to PPR cells at ss4/8 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the gene module expression patterns across stages.

claim: Principal component 1 (PC1) at HH7 provides an axis representing the mediolateral position of cells in vivo.
source: We chose to model the spatial expression of 'NPB specifiers' using our HH7 scRNAseq data as this stage marks the start of placodal and neural crest segregation (Figure 3A). Principal component analysis reveals that HH7 cells are ordered along the principal component (PC) 1 based on their M-L position in vivo; PC1 therefore provides an axis through which we can model spatial gene expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A where cell states are distributed along PC1 according to their mediolateral position.

claim: Msx1 and Pax7 are upregulated medially relative to Dlx6 and Six1.
source: Our models predict that Msx1 and Pax7 are upregulated medially relative to Dlx6 and Six1, in line with their roles in neural crest and placodal specification, respectively (Basch et al., 2006; Brugmann et al., 2004; Christophorou et al., 2009; McLarren et al., 2003; Monsoro-Burq et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on the spatial gene expression modeling shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pax7 and Six1 exhibit a smaller region of co-expression with each other than with either Msx1 or Dlx6.
source: Interestingly, Pax7 and Six1, which are upregulated later than either Msx1 and Dlx6 (Figure 3E), are predicted to exhibit a smaller region of co-expression with each other than with either Msx1 or Dlx6 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on the spatial gene expression modeling and validated by HCR.

claim: Tfap2a overlaps extensively with both Pax7 and Six1.
source: Tfap2a, which is required for both placodal and neural crest specification (Bhat et al., 2013; Rothstein and Simoes-Costa, 2020), is predicted to overlap extensively with both Pax7 and Six1.
evidence: This is based on the spatial gene expression modeling shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HCR validates the predicted levels of co-expression across the M-L axis in vivo.
source: HCR at the same stage validates the predicted levels of co-expression across the M-L axis in vivo (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is shown by the HCR images and intensity measurements in Figure 5C-E.

claim: There are clear differences in co-expression of NPB markers along the A-P axis.
source: Importantly, we show that there are clear differences in their co-expression along the A-P axis.
evidence: This is shown by the intensity measurements at different A-P levels in Figure 5D.

claim: Dlx6 and Six1 are strongly expressed anteriorly.
source: While Dlx6 and Six1 are strongly expressed anteriorly, Pax7 and Msx1 show increased expression levels posteriorly (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the intensity measurements in Figure 5D.

claim: Pax7 and Msx1 show increased expression levels posteriorly.
source: While Dlx6 and Six1 are strongly expressed anteriorly, Pax7 and Msx1 show increased expression levels posteriorly (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the intensity measurements in Figure 5D.

claim: A unique NPB cell state cannot be defined transcriptionally using previously established criteria.
source: Together, these results highlight that whilst the NPB can be defined as a territory adjacent to the developing neural plate, a unique NPB cell state cannot be defined transcriptionally using previously established criteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial expression analysis and co-expression patterns.

claim: Undecided multi-potent progenitors often transition through an intermediate state characterised by high transcriptional heterogeneity and co-expression of competing transcriptional programmes.
source: Recent studies in other systems have revealed that undecided multi-potent progenitors often transition through an intermediate state characterised by high transcriptional heterogeneity and co-expression of competing transcriptional programmes (Soldatov et al., 2019; Subkhankulova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies in other systems.

claim: GM10 contains the canonical forebrain markers Hesx1 and Six3.
source: GM10 is upregulated in the forebrain and contains the canonical forebrain markers Hesx1 and Six3.
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis.

claim: GM16 is enriched within mid-hindbrain clusters and expresses known mid-hindbrain markers Sp5 and Nkx6-2.
source: GM16 is enriched within mid-hindbrain clusters and expresses known mid-hindbrain markers Sp5 and Nkx6-2; this module also exhibits low levels of expression in other neural clusters, but importantly, is downregulated in the neural crest.
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis.

claim: GM5 contains well-characterised placodal markers including Six1, Homer2, and Znf385c.
source: GM5 contains well-characterised placodal markers including Six1, Homer2, and Znf385c and is expressed in both aPPR and pPPR clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis.

claim: GM2 contains neural crest specifiers including FoxD3, Snai2, Sox9, Pax7, and Msx1, as well as the Wnt ligands Wnt1 and Wnt6.
source: GM2 is expressed in both neural crest and delaminating neural crest clusters and contains neural crest specifiers including FoxD3, Snai2, Sox9, Pax7, and Msx1, as well as the Wnt ligands Wnt1 and Wnt6.
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis.

claim: At head process stages (HH5) almost all cells co-express all gene modules suggesting broad multipotency.
source: At head process stages (HH5) almost all cells co-express all gene modules suggesting broad multipotency.
evidence: This is shown in the co-expression analysis in Figure 6.

claim: At later stages (ss4 and ss8) only small subsets of cells retain high levels of co-expression of multiple fate modules.
source: At later stages (ss4 and ss8) only small subsets of cells retain high levels of co-expression (Figure 6C' and D', dashed boxes).
evidence: This is shown in the co-expression histograms in Figure 6C', D', and E'.

claim: The shift from broad to restricted co-expression suggests that ectodermal fates segregate between HH7 and ss8.
source: This shift from broad to restricted co-expression suggests that ectodermal fate segregate between HH7 and ss8.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-expression distribution changes over time.

claim: At the placodal/neural crest boundary, cells continue to co-express all four gene modules, indicating they may retain the potential to give rise to all four fates.
source: At the placodal/neural crest boundary, cells continue to co-express all four gene modules, albeit at different levels indicating that they may retain the potential to give rise to all four fates (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is shown in the co-expression analysis in Figure 6C-E.

claim: BLUPs are transcriptionally undecided and co-express gene modules that characterise alternative ectodermal fates.
source: Overall, our co-expression analysis highlights that BLUPs are transcriptionally undecided and co-express gene modules that characterise alternative ectodermal fates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-expression analysis.

claim: The proportion of BLUPs decreases over time, but a small population at ss4 retains this characteristic.
source: The proportion of these cells decreases over time, but a small population at ss4 retains this characteristic and is therefore likely to retain bi- or multipotency even as the neural tube closes.
evidence: This is shown in the co-expression analysis across developmental stages.

claim: GM12 contains early non-neural/PPR markers like Gata2/3.
source: GM12 is expressed throughout both aPPR and pNPB and contains early non-neural/PPR markers like Gata2/3 (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis of the NPB subset.

claim: GM14 contains pan-placodal genes Dlx5/6 as well as anterior markers Six3 and Pax6.
source: Unlike GM12, GM14 is initially restricted to the PPR and only activated in the pNPB at HH7. At ss4 and ss8 its expression is confined to the PPR, with a higher expression in anterior cells. This module contains pan-placodal genes Dlx5/6 as well as anterior markers Six3 and Pax6.
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis of the NPB subset.

claim: GM13 contains the definitive placodal transcripts Six1 and Eya2.
source: GM13 is the last placodal module to be activated and contains the definitive placodal transcripts Six1 and Eya2.
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis of the NPB subset.

claim: GM12 is activated before GM14 and GM13 in latent time within placodal cells.
source: This analysis shows that GM12 is activated before GM14 and GM13 in latent time.
evidence: This is shown in the gene module dynamics modeling in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The four neural crest gene modules contain bona fide neural crest transcriptional regulators including Msx1, Zic1, Zeb2, Lmx1b (GM40), Pax7, Snai2, Axud1, Foxd3, Tfap2b, Sox9 (GM42), Sox5, Id1/2 (GM44) and Sox10, Ets1, Lmo4 and Sox8 (GM43).
source: The four neural crest gene modules each contain bona fide neural crest transcriptional regulators including Msx1, Zic1, Zeb2, Lmx1b (GM40), Pax7, Snai2, Axud1, Foxd3, Tfap2b, Sox9 (GM42), Sox5, Id1/2 (GM44) and Sox10, Ets1, Lmo4 and Sox8 (GM43) (Figure 7E and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the gene module analysis of the NPB subset.

claim: Neural crest gene modules show a clear sequential activation from GM40 to GM42, GM44, and GM43.
source: Our analysis groups these factors unbiasedly into four modules; modelling their expression across latent time weighted by neural crest fate probability shows a clear sequential activation from GM40 to GM42, GM44, and GM43 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the gene module dynamics modeling in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ass1 and Six1 are co-localised within the lateral NPB at HH7 and ss4, and in the otic placode at HH11.
source: HCR confirms that Ass1 and Six1 are co-localised within the lateral NPB at HH7 and ss4, and in the otic placode at HH11 (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is shown by HCR validation in Figure 7G.

claim: Ass1 is initially upregulated in both placodal and early neural crest cells before being downregulated in the neural crest.
source: These experiments also reveal a greater degree in co-expression of Pax7/Ass1 than Pax7/Six1 (Figure 7G; HH7 and ss4). in line with our dynamic gene expression modelling, which predicts that Ass1 is initially upregulated in both placodal and early neural crest cells before being downregulated in the neural crest (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: This is shown by HCR validation and gene dynamics modeling in Figure 7G, H, and I.

claim: Olfml3 is upregulated within the neural crest in between Pax7 and Sox10.
source: Olfml3 was chosen as a novel neural crest marker, as it is found in GM44 which is predicted to be upregulated within the neural crest in between GM42 (Pax7) and GM43 (Sox10) (Figure 7H). HCR confirmed the predicted sequential expression of these markers, with Pax7 active in the posterior NPB at HH7, Pax7, and Olfml3 co-expressed at NPB at ss4, and all three markers expressed within the neural crest at HH11 when the neural crest is undergoing delamination (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown by HCR validation in Figure 7F and gene dynamics modeling in Figure 7H.

claim: The development of the neural crest and neural fates requires the downregulation of the epiblast signatures prior to the activation of neural and neural crest modules.
source: Given that the expression of epiblast modules becomes confined to the placodes later, we speculate that the development of the neural crest and neural fates requires the downregulation of the epiblast signatures prior to the activation of neural and neural crest modules.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed expression dynamics of epiblast modules.

claim: The NPB is an ectodermal territory surrounding the neural plate that contains cells with heterogeneous combinations of gene expression.
source: Here, we show that the NPB is an ectodermal territory surrounding the neural plate that contains cells with heterogeneous combinations of gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial expression analysis and co-expression patterns.

claim: NPB cells are characterised by the co-expression of gene modules which regulate the specification of alternative cell fates suggesting that they are undecided progenitors.
source: These cells are characterised by the co-expression of gene modules which regulate the specification of alternative cell fates suggesting that they are undecided progenitors.
evidence: This is based on the co-expression analysis of gene modules.

claim: At the 4-somite stage, cells co-express placodal and forebrain modules, but not neural crest modules.
source: Our co-expression analysis reveals that at the 4-somite stage, cells co-express placodal and forebrain modules, but not neural crest modules.
evidence: This is shown in the co-expression analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: At the 4-somite stage, other cells co-express neural and neural crest, but not placodal modules.
source: In contrast, other cells co-express neural and neural crest, but not placodal modules, while a small subset of cells at the branching point between neural crest and placodes co-express modules characteristic for all three ectodermal fates (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the co-expression analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: A small subset of cells at the branching point between neural crest and placodes co-express modules characteristic for all three ectodermal fates at the 4-somite stage.
source: In contrast, other cells co-express neural and neural crest, but not placodal modules, while a small subset of cells at the branching point between neural crest and placodes co-express modules characteristic for all three ectodermal fates (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the co-expression analysis in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The NPB should be viewed as a region of ectoderm surrounding the developing neural plate, where cells of undecided fates reside.
source: In summary, rather than considering the NPB as a unique territory of equivalent cells it should be viewed as a region of ectoderm surrounding the developing neural plate, where cells of undecided fates reside.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of cell heterogeneity and co-expression patterns.

claim: The probabilistic model proposes that medial NPB cells are more likely to generate neural crest and neural cells while lateral NPB cells have the propensity to produce epidermis and placodal derivatives.
source: We therefore propose a probabilistic model for cell fate allocation at the NPB which considers levels of gene expression and the position of cells (Figure 8). According to this model medial NPB cells are more likely to generate neural crest and neural cells while lateral NPB cells have the propensity to produce epidermis and placodal derivatives.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the spatial expression patterns and co-expression analysis.

claim: Cells in the centre of the NPB retain multipotency and continue to be in an undecided state with equal possibility to give rise to all four ectodermal derivatives.
source: In contrast, cells in the centre of the NPB retain multipotency and continue to be in an undecided state with equal possibility to give rise to all four ectodermal derivatives.
evidence: This is part of the proposed probabilistic model based on co-expression patterns.

claim: Samples were collected over multiple days and stored in 90% MeOH with 10% resuspension solution after FAC sorting.
source: Given the low number of cells obtained from each embryo, samples for each stage were collected over multiple days and stored in 90% MeOH with 10% resuspension solution after FAC sorting.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Library preparation was carried out using the 10x3' single-cell mRNA v3 kit.
source: Library preparation was carried out using the 10x3' single-cell mRNA v3 kit (10 x Genomics), before sequencing on the HiSeq 4000 (Illumina) to a target depth of 50 k reads/cell.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Samples were sequenced on the HiSeq 4000 to a target depth of 50 k reads/cell.
source: Library preparation was carried out using the 10x3' single-cell mRNA v3 kit (10 x Genomics), before sequencing on the HiSeq 4000 (Illumina) to a target depth of 50 k reads/cell.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Reads were processed and aligned to GalGal6 using CellRanger 4.0.0.
source: Reads were processed and aligned to GalGal6 using CellRanger 4.0.0 (10x Genomics).
evidence: This is a description of the bioinformatics methodology.

claim: Quality control, data filtering, cell clustering, dimensionality reduction and initial data visualisation was carried out using Seurat v4.0.5.
source: Quality control, data filtering, cell clustering, dimensionality reduction and initial data visualisation was carried out using Seurat v4.0.5 (Hao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the bioinformatics methodology.

claim: Cells from the two separate batches were integrated into a single full dataset using STACAS v1.1.0.
source: After the removal of poor-quality cells, cells from the two separate batches were integrated into a single full dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I). To avoid over-correction and removal of stage differences, we integrated the data from the two sequencing batches using STACAS v1.1.0 (Andreatta and Carmona, 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the data integration methodology.

claim: Percentage mitochondrial content, cell sex, and cell cycle were regressed out before downstream analysis.
source: Before downstream analysis, we regressed out percentage mitochondrial content, cell sex, and cell cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the data normalization methodology.

claim: RNA velocity was calculated using scVelo with the dynamical model whilst accounting for differential kinetics.
source: RNA velocity was ran using the dynamical model whilst accounting for differential kinetics; this allows for differential splicing rates between genes as well as differential splicing kinetics between cell states.
evidence: This is a description of the RNA velocity methodology.

claim: Lineage inference was calculated using CellRank, which uses a probabilistic approach to assign cell lineage.
source: Lineage inference was calculated using CellRank, which uses a probabilistic approach to assign cell lineage (Lange et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a description of the lineage inference methodology.

claim: Gene expression dynamics were calculated by fitting generalised additive models (GAMs), which modelled average normalised gene expression as a function of latent time using the mgcv package in R.
source: Gene expression dynamics were calculated by fitting generalised additive models (GAMs), which modelled average normalised gene expression as a function of latent time using the mgcv package in R.
evidence: This is a description of the gene expression dynamics modeling methodology.
